newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--New CEO eyes licensing to boost Donna Karan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--New CEO eyes licensing to boost Donna Karan.

text.p: Donna Karan International Inc's newly named chief executive aims to capitalize on the designer's brand name with lucrative licensing deals to pull the designer's stock out of its slump.

The 38-year-old executive, John Idol, comes to the troubled design house with strong credentials -- he helped develop the Ralph Lauren name during his 13 year tenure into one of the leading designer brands through licensing pacts.
Most recently, he oversaw clothes, sheets, furniture and paint, among others, that accounted for $1.7 billion in annual revenues at Polo Ralph Lauren Corp.

Idol said his first priorities at Donna Karan are to increase shareholder value and profitability, particularly through licensing deals but also by building more stand-alone stores in both the United States and abroad. There are currently over 50 stores abroad and the company will open its first domestic store in Las Vegas around Thanksgiving.
"We plan to further exploit the opportunity of licensing alliances in the future. There is definitely an opportunity to grow that category," Idol told Reuters in a phone interview.
He takes on the job from Donna Karan, who remains chairwoman and chief designer.
Analysts say the stickiest part of his new job may be negotiating with Karan herself, who is known for a very hands-on approach to her business.

"Idol comes with an impeccable pedigree. Ralph Lauren is one of the most successful U.S. designers and is the all-time champ in terms of licensing revenues. But the question is how much responsibility will he really have and how they work together on a day-to-day basis, " said Alan Millstein, editor and publisher of the Fashion Network, an industry newsletter.
The news of the new executive seemed to give hope to investors, sending the stock up 1-1/8 to at 11-9/16 in midday New York Stock Exchange trade.

"He has to rein in costs in a big way, put the name on a lot of products and distribute through channels they haven't used before. He is likely to have the business acumen to bring the company on a sound financial footing and expand from there," said Kurt Barnard, editor of Barnard's Retail Marketing Report.
Donna Karan said she was confident in her choice and said Idol would have "full authority to lead and manage" the company.

"We worked hard to find the right person, one who I felt totally confident in and could really build the brand. I feel a lot more comfortable being able to concentrate my energies on what I do best -- design," she told Reuters.
"I really believe John is the right person to carry out our vision," she said.
Donna Karan International has been struggling since it went public a year ago.
Shareholders have seen their investments lose nearly a third of their value, slumping from a debut price of $24 all the way down to 8-7/16.
In May the company announced a restructuring that included a four percent cut in its workforce, a hiring freeze and steps to reduce its expenses by $4.8 million.
Some of the shareholders slapped the company with a lawsuit in June, alleging the designer failed to disclose cost-control problems and hurt its income and ability to grow. Other
analysts had grumbled in the past too that perhaps Donna Karan, a designer by trade, should allow a more experienced business hand at the till.

In naming Idol as chief executive, the company bypassed its own chief operating officer and president Stephen Ruzow. Originally, the designer said it planned to name a co-chief executive officer with Ruzow but gave Idol the sole title. Ruzow will report to Idol.
